appeal.letter:
Subject: Appeal against Denial D03 – Pre‑Existing Disease Waiting Period (Claim ID: 922fb35e-148d-9e82-ef97-76365a73dff8)

Claim Details:  
Patient Name: Agnes Laree Weber  
Patient ID: 922fb35e-148d-9e82-7e65-bfa05e3b3515  
Date of Service: 2024‑10‑28 (Follow‑up encounter, Ambulatory)  
Diagnosis: Essential hypertension (onset 2024‑05‑31)  
Procedure: Follow‑up encounter (cardiac category)  
Plan: Suraksha Silver Individual Health Plan (SGH‑SILVER) – Coverage effective 2024‑05‑03  
Claim Amount: INR 342.20  

Grounds for Appeal:  
The insurer’s denial is based on a presumed pre‑existing disease waiting period. Under the policy definition, a Pre‑Existing Disease is a condition diagnosed or treated within 48 months prior to the first policy start date. Essential hypertension for this patient was first diagnosed on 31 May 2024, which is after the policy start date of 3 May 2024. Accordingly, the condition does not meet the definition of a Pre‑Existing Disease and the 36‑month waiting period does not apply [suraksha_silver_policy#5]. The waiting‑period clause itself applies only to conditions that satisfy that definition, and therefore does not cover this diagnosis [suraksha_silver_policy#11].

Burden of Proof:  
According to the claims procedure and grievance guidelines, the insurer bears the burden of proving that an exclusion or waiting period is applicable and must provide documentary evidence of a prior diagnosis. No such evidence has been presented for this claim [claims_procedure_and_grievance#6].

Clinical Necessity:  
Essential hypertension requires regular monitoring to prevent serious complications such as stroke, heart failure, and kidney disease. Clinical guidance recommends follow‑up reviews every 4–6 weeks after diagnosis or medication change, with ongoing monitoring of blood pressure, electrolytes, creatinine, and target‑organ assessment [hypertension#3]. The follow‑up encounter submitted under this claim is consistent with these medical standards.

Reference to Denial Standards:  
The denial was issued under standard D03, yet the insurer has not satisfied the required burden of proof for a pre‑existing disease exclusion, as stipulated in the grievance redressal standards [claims_procedure_and_grievance#6].

Request:  
In light of the above, we respectfully request that the denial be withdrawn, the claim be reprocessed, and the amount of INR 342.20 be paid in full to the provider.

Thank you for your prompt attention to this matter.

Insurance Desk (on behalf of the treating provider)

citations.section: Suraksha Silver Individual Health Plan (Policy Wording) > 4. Waiting Periods > 4.2 Pre-Existing Disease Waiting Period
citations.quote:
### 4.2 Pre-Existing Disease Waiting Period
Expenses related to a Pre-Existing Disease (as defined in Clause 2.2) are covered only after 36 months of continuous coverage from the first policy start date. This waiting period applies ONLY to conditions meeting the definition in Clause 2.2.

citations.section: Suraksha Silver Individual Health Plan (Policy Wording) > 2. Definitions > 2.2 Pre-Existing Disease (PED)
citations.quote:
### 2.2 Pre-Existing Disease (PED)
Pre-Existing Disease means any condition, ailment, injury or disease that was diagnosed by a physician, or for which medical advice or treatment was received, within 48 months PRIOR TO the first policy start date. A condition that is first diagnosed ON OR AFTER the policy start date is NOT a Pre-Existing Disease, irrespective of whether the condition is chronic i

citations.section: Claims Procedure, Denial Standards and Grievance Redressal > C3. Standards for Denial > C3.2 Burden of Proof for Exclusions and Waiting Periods
citations.quote:
### C3.2 Burden of Proof for Exclusions and Waiting Periods
The insurer bears the burden of proving that an exclusion or waiting period applies. For a Pre-Existing Disease denial, the insurer must show documentary evidence that the condition was diagnosed or treated before the policy start date.

citations.section: Essential Hypertension — Diagnosis and Monitoring > Medical Necessity of Monitoring
citations.quote:
## Medical Necessity of Monitoring
After diagnosis or a medication change, review every 4–6 weeks until controlled, then every 3–6 months. Monitoring includes blood pressure measurement, electrolytes and creatinine, and screening for target-organ damage (ECG, urine albumin). Regular monitoring prevents stroke, heart failure and kidney disease.
